Ayrıca: {source:29:59} "yalnız bana kulluk edin" çağrısının muhataplarının sabreden ve yalnız Rablerine dayananlar diye anılması; {source:6:102} kulluk emrinin ardından O'nun her şeye vekil oluşu; {source:17:2} {source:33:3} {source:73:9} vekil, yani dayanılacak olan olarak yalnız O'nun edinilmesi; {source:14:35} İbrahim'in kendisini ve oğullarını putlara kulluktan uzak tutması için Rabbine dua etmesi, kulluğun kendisi için istenen yardım; {source:2:45} namazın huşû duyanlardan başkasına ağır gelmesi, kulluğun yükü; {source:2:286} gücün yetmediği yükün yüklenmemesinin istenmesi

Burada beklenmedik bir şey ortaya çıkar. Kur'an, yardım istenecek şeyler arasında namazı da sayar. Önce İsrailoğullarına {ar:وَٱسْتَعِينُوا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِ ۚ وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلْخَٰشِعِينَ, tr:vesteînû bi's-sabri ve's-salâh, ve innehâ le-kebîratün ille ale'l-hâşi'în, gloss:sabırla ve namazla yardım isteyin; o, gönülden boyun eğenlerden başkasına ağır gelir, source:2:45} denir. Sonra müminlere {ar:يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱسْتَعِينُوا۟ بِٱلصَّبْرِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِ, tr:yâ eyyühe'llezîne âmenü'steînû bi's-sabri ve's-salâh, gloss:ey iman edenler, sabırla ve namazla yardım isteyin, source:2:153} denir. Fâtiha her namazda okunur. Kişi "yardımı yalnız senden dileriz" sözünü, kendisi bir dayanak olan namazın içinde söyler. Yardım isteği, istenen yardımın içinde yapılmış olur. Görünürdeki çelişki de "avn" kelimesinin genişliğiyle çözülür. Sabır ve namaz insanın dayandığı araçlardır, yardımı istenen ise yalnız O'dur. Musa, Firavun'un oğulları öldürme tehdidi karşısında {source:7:127} halkına bu iki şeyi ayrı ayrı söyler: {ar:ٱسْتَعِينُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱصْبِرُوٓا۟, tr:isteînû billâhi vasbirû, gloss:Allah'tan yardım isteyin ve sabredin, source:7:128}. Yardım Allah'tan istenir, sabretmek ise onların işidir.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=17 kind=prose ref=7:126 -->
A'râf suresinde, Musa'nın bu sözünden hemen önce, iman eden sihirbazlar Firavun'un el ve ayaklarını çaprazlama kesip hepsini asma tehdidiyle karşılaşır {source:7:124}. Onlar bu tehdide şu duayla karşılık verir: {ar:رَبَّنَآ أَفْرِغْ عَلَيْنَا صَبْرًۭا وَتَوَفَّنَا مُسْلِمِينَ, tr:rabbenâ efrig aleynâ sabran ve teveffenâ müslimîn, gloss:Rabbimiz, üzerimize sabır boşalt ve canımızı müslümanlar olarak al, source:7:126}. Musa'nın sözünde kavme kendi işi olarak emredilen sabır, burada Rabden dilenen bir bağış olarak istenir.

Bağışlanma diledikten sonra {source:28:16} şu sözü verir: {ar:رَبِّ بِمَآ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَىَّ فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيرًۭا لِّلْمُجْرِمِينَ, tr:rabbi bimâ en'amte aleyye fe-len ekûne zahîran li'l-mücrimîn, gloss:Rabbim, bana verdiğin nimet hakkı için suçlulara asla arka çıkmayacağım, source:28:17}. Bu sözde yedinci ayetteki "en'amte" ile yardımın "zahîr" kelimesi aynı cümlede yer alır. Nimeti tanıyan kişi kime arka çıkacağını da seçer.

Tâhâ suresinde Firavun'a gitmekle görevlendirilen {source:20:24} Musa, bir insandan gelecek yardımı da Rabbinden ister. Ailesinden kardeşi Harun'un kendisine yardımcı kılınmasını, onunla gücünün pekiştirilmesini ve onun işine ortak edilmesini diler {source:20:29} {source:20:30} {source:20:31} {source:20:32}. Yardım yalnızca tek yönde akar. Allah'tan başka çağrılanlar için şöyle denir: {ar:وَمَا لَهُۥ مِنْهُم مِّن ظَهِيرٍۢ, tr:ve mâ lehû minhüm min zahîr, gloss:O'nun onlardan bir destekçisi de yoktur, source:34:22}. Hamd sözü de bunu tamamlar: {ar:وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُۥ وَلِىٌّۭ مِّنَ ٱلذُّلِّ, tr:ve lem yekün lehû veliyyün mine'z-züll, gloss:güçsüzlükten ötürü bir yardımcıya da ihtiyacı olmadı, source:17:111}. Kulluğun tanımında geçen "tezellül", yani boyun eğiş, kula aittir. Allah hakkında aynı kökten gelen "züll", yani düşkünlük, açıkça reddedilir. Kul kulluğunu ve yardım isteğini O'na yöneltir. O ise ne birinin kulu olur ne de birinin yardımına muhtaç olur.

Öyleyse rızkı Allah katında arayın, O'na kulluk edin ve O'na şükredin, source:29:17}. Kulluk edilenlerin elinde verecek bir şey yoktur. ## "Biz"

İki fiil de çoğuldur: kulluk ederiz, yardım dileriz. Fâtiha her namazda okunduğu için kişi yalnız namaz kıldığında da "ben" değil "biz" der. Allah'ın kulları kelimesi bir topluluğu da anlatır. Kur'an'daki bir davet bu yüzden {ar:فادخلي في عبادي أي في حزبي, tr:fe'dhulî fî ibâdî ey fî hizbî, gloss:kullarımın arasına gir, yani benim topluluğuma katıl, source:"ع ب د,B002"} diye açıklanır. Bu davet, yeryüzünün dövülüp düzlendiği ve Rabbin meleklerle saf saf geldiği günün anlatıldığı yerde geçer {source:89:22}. Allah orada huzura ermiş cana seslenir: {ar:يَٰٓأَيَّتُهَا ٱلنَّفْسُ ٱلْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ, tr:yâ eyyetühe'n-nefsü'l-mutmainne, gloss:ey huzura ermiş can, source:89:27}. Ona Rabbine dönmesini söyler {source:89:28}, sonra şöyle der: {ar:فَٱدْخُلِى فِى عِبَٰدِى, tr:fedhulî fî ibâdî, gloss:kullarımın arasına gir, source:89:29}. Bahçeye girmek {ar:وَٱدْخُلِى جَنَّتِى, tr:vedhulî cennetî, gloss:cennetime gir, source:89:30} ancak bundan sonra gelir. Varılan yerin ilk adı bir topluluktur. Beşinci ayetin "biz"i o topluluğun dünyada söylediği sözdür.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=20 kind=prose ref=2:133 -->
Bakara suresi bu "biz"i nesiller boyunca uzatır. Ölüm Yakup'a geldiğinde oğullarına kendisinden sonra neye kulluk edeceklerini sorar. Şu cevabı alır: {ar:قَالُوا۟ نَعْبُدُ إِلَٰهَكَ وَإِلَٰهَ ءَابَآئِكَ إِبْرَٰهِۦمَ وَإِسْمَٰعِيلَ وَإِسْحَٰقَ إِلَٰهًۭا وَٰحِدًۭا وَنَحْنُ لَهُۥ مُسْلِمُونَ, tr:kâlû na'büdü ilâheke ve ilâhe âbâike İbrâhîme ve İsmâîle ve İshâka ilâhen vâhidâ, ve nahnü lehû müslimûn, gloss:dediler ki: Senin ilahına, ataların İbrahim, İsmail ve İshak'ın ilahına, tek bir ilaha kulluk ederiz; biz O'na teslim olmuşuz, source:2:133}. Fâtiha'daki fiil burada aynı biçimiyle, "na'büdü" olarak gelir. Onu söyleyen "biz", ölüm döşeğindeki babayı ve ondan önceki ataları da içine alır.

<!-- v16:augment brief=augment9 model=opus para=20 kind=refs -->
Ayrıca: {source:89:21} yeryüzünün dövülüp düzlenmesi; {source:2:43} rükû edenlerle birlikte rükû, kulluğun toplulukla yapılması; {source:2:138} "biz O'na kulluk edenleriz" diyen topluluk; {source:18:14} kalkıp "Rabbimiz göklerin ve yerin Rabbidir, O'ndan başka ilaha asla yalvarmayız" diyen gençlerin "biz"i; {source:27:19} Süleyman'ın "rahmetinle beni salih kullarının arasına kat" duası; {source:4:69} Allah'a ve elçiye itaat edenlerin Allah'ın nimet verdikleriyle birlikte olması ve "ne güzel arkadaştırlar" denmesi; {source:2:286} müminlerin baştan sona "biz" ağzından Allah'a "sen" diye seslenen duası; {source:11:62} atalarının kulluk ettiğine bağlı kalan karşıt "biz"

Bu "biz" dışarıya kapalı değildir. Daha önce kitap ehline yöneltilen çağrı "kulluk etmeyelim" diye birinci çoğul şahısla kurulmuştu. Yani aynı fiilin "biz"i, ayrı yollardan gelenleri ortak bir söze çağırır. Topluluğun kendi içindeki yardımlaşması da aynı kökten gelir: "teâvenû", yani iyilikte birbirinize yardım edin. Aynı harfler yaban eşeği sürüsüne de ad verir: {ar:العانة القطيع من حمر الوحش, tr:el-ânetü'l-katî'u min humuri'l-vahş, gloss:âne, yaban eşeği sürüsüdür, source:"ع و ن,B006"}. Bu kelime, birlikte koşan bir sürüden öte bir şey taşımaz. Ayetteki "biz" ise sahibini bilen ve O'na "sen" diye seslenen bir topluluktur.

Bu topluluğa ait olmak bir korumadır. İblis insanları yoldan çıkaracağına yemin ettiğinde kendisi bir istisna yapar: {ar:إِلَّا عِبَادَكَ مِنْهُمُ ٱلْمُخْلَصِينَ, tr:illâ ibâdeke minhümü'l-muhlasîn, gloss:onlardan ancak arınmış kulların hariç, source:15:40}. Allah da ona cevap verir: {ar:إِنَّ عِبَادِى لَيْسَ لَكَ عَلَيْهِمْ سُلْطَٰنٌ, tr:inne ibâdî leyse leke aleyhim sultân, gloss:kullarım üzerinde senin hiçbir gücün yoktur, source:15:42}. Tek sahibe ait olduğunu kendi ağzıyla söyleyen kişi, başka bir efendinin eline düşmez. Firavun'un saray adamlarının "bize kulluk ediyorlar" dediği halk, Fâtiha'nın her okunuşunda bu sözün tersini söyler: Biz yalnız sana kulluk ederiz.

payload.input:
const cmd = `cat > enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_5/luna/list.tsv <<'EOF'
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Deut.6.13\tʿbd service root\tThe commentary labels naʿbudu with Arabic ʿ-b-d; Deuteronomy uses the cognate Hebrew ʿābad for serving YHWH alone, showing the same service and worship range.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Deut.6.13\texclusive service\tThe commentary stresses that the foregrounded “you” excludes every other object of worship; Deut 6:13 commands Israel to fear and serve YHWH alone.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Deut.6.4\tone God\tThe commentary makes exclusive address the point of “you alone”; the Shema confesses YHWH as Israel’s one God, grounding that exclusivity in Israel’s central creed.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Ps.100.2\tʿbd service root\tThe commentary labels naʿbudu from Arabic ʿ-b-d; Psalm 100 uses Hebrew ʿābad for the community’s joyful service of YHWH as it comes before him with song.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.100.3\tpeople and flock\tThe commentary treats “we” as a community that knows its owner; the psalm names worshippers as God’s people and sheep of his pasture, giving communal service a shepherd-and-flock image.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Exod.3.12\tʿbd service root\tThe commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d is cognate with the Hebrew root in “you shall serve God”; Exodus makes service to God the destination of Israel’s release from Egypt.
strong\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Exod.3.12\tIsrael freed to serve\tThe commentary recalls Pharaoh’s enslavement of Israel and its reversal in exclusive service to God; Moses is told that the people will serve God on this mountain after leaving Egypt.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Exod.1.14\tʿbd forced labor\tThe commentary links ʿabd to both belonging and enslavement; Exodus uses the cognate Hebrew service word for Israel’s bitter forced labor under Egypt.
strong\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Exod.1.14\tPharaoh’s enslavement\tThe commentary’s Pharaoh scene treats human mastery as the corrupt form of servitude; Exodus describes the Egyptians making Israel’s life bitter with hard labor.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Lev.25.42\tʿbd and ownership\tThe commentary calls the worshipper God’s owned servant; Leviticus calls Israelites God’s servants, brought out of Egypt, and forbids selling them as slaves.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Deut.10.12\tʿbd and walking\tThe commentary links service with a trodden, guided way; Deut 10:12 puts walking in God’s ways beside serving him with all one’s heart and soul.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Deut.10.12\twalk and serve\tThe commentary hears a path within service and then asks for guidance; Moses joins walking in God’s ways to loving and serving him wholeheartedly.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Deut.11.13\tʿbd with all the heart\tThe commentary describes worship as an all-encompassing allegiance; Deut 11:13 uses the cognate Hebrew service root in a command to love and serve YHWH with all heart and soul.
strong\ttevrat\tsoydas\tWLC:Josh.24.15\tʿbd service root\tThe commentary’s naʿbudu and Joshua’s “we will serve YHWH” use cognate Arabic and Hebrew roots for service.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Josh.24.15\tour household’s choice\tThe commentary reads “we” as a worshipping community; Joshua sets rival gods before Israel and declares that he and his household will serve YHWH.
strong\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Gen.35.2\tremove other gods\tThe commentary makes the worshipper’s exclusive choice rule out other masters; Jacob tells his whole household to put away foreign gods before going to Bethel.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Gen.35.3\tworship and answered distress\tThe commentary joins service and asking help in one first-person plural prayer; Jacob calls the household to make an altar to the God who answered him in distress and stayed with him on the way.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:1Kgs.18.21\tdivided allegiance\tThe commentary contrasts one owner with competing masters; Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between two opinions and calls for a decision between YHWH and Baal.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.86.10\tyou alone are God\tThe commentary’s fronted “you” excludes all other recipients of worship; the psalmist addresses God as great and says that he alone is God.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.50.15\tcall and honor\tThe commentary distinguishes asking God for aid from the means used to endure; Psalm 50 joins calling on God in trouble, his deliverance, and the worshipper’s honoring him.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.50.12\tGod needs no aid\tThe commentary says God is not a servant or a needy recipient of help; Psalm 50 says God would not need to tell Israel if he were hungry because the world is his.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.121.2\thelper and creator\tThe commentary leaves the requested aid open to every need; the pilgrim psalm names YHWH, maker of heaven and earth, as the speaker’s help.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.95.6\tbowing before God\tThe commentary explains service as obedience reaching humility; the psalm calls the community to bow and kneel before its maker.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.95.7\twe under God’s hand\tThe commentary’s “we” is a community belonging to one owner; the psalm calls Israel God’s people and the sheep of his hand.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.115.9\tcommunity trusts God for help\tThe commentary speaks for a plural worshipping community that asks only God for aid; the psalm tells Israel to trust YHWH, its help and shield.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Neh.9.6\tyou alone, creator, worshipped\tThe commentary moves from praise of God to direct address and exclusive service; Nehemiah’s communal prayer says “you alone” are YHWH, maker of all, while heaven’s host worships you.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Neh.9.32\tour God, communal plea\tThe commentary has a praying “we” address God directly for aid; Nehemiah’s communal confession turns to “our God” and asks him to attend to the people’s hardship.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.46.4\tGod carries his people\tThe commentary’s aid includes support for the worn traveler; Isaiah contrasts idols that must be carried with God’s promise to carry and rescue Israel from birth to old age.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.46.7\tidols cannot answer\tThe commentary asks why help should be sought from what cannot benefit or save; Isaiah says an idol cannot answer its worshippers or rescue them from trouble.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:1Kgs.18.26\tcalling idols without help\tThe commentary says false objects of worship cannot provide aid; in Elijah’s contest Baal’s prophets call and dance, but no voice answers them.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.40.3\tprepare a way\tThe commentary develops the worked, passable road as an image beside service and guidance; Isaiah calls for a way to be prepared for the Lord’s coming.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.40.4\tlevel the road\tThe commentary describes a road made easy by being flattened; Isaiah pictures valleys raised and rough ground leveled to make the Lord’s highway passable.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.56.6\tforeigners join God’s servants\tThe commentary says the first-person plural community is open to people from different paths; Isaiah includes foreigners who join themselves to YHWH, serve him, and love his name.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Exod.17.12\thuman hands strengthen the weary\tThe commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from human agents who can assist; Aaron and Hur physically support Moses’ hands when he grows tired.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Eccl.4.10\thelping the fallen traveler\tThe commentary evokes a traveler whose mount fails and who needs support; Qoheleth says a companion can lift someone who falls, making human aid concrete beneath reliance on God.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:2Chr.19.2\twrongly supporting the wicked\tThe commentary warns that backing someone can aid wrongdoing; Jehu rebukes Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked and loving those who hate YHWH.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.4.10\tserve and worship God alone\tThe commentary emphasizes that “you alone” excludes every rival recipient; Jesus answers the tempter by commanding worship and service of the Lord God alone.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.9\tcommunal direct address\tThe commentary stresses the turn from speaking about God to speaking to him, and the plural “we”; Jesus teaches disciples to begin prayer with “Our Father.”
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.11\tasking God for provision\tThe commentary says the second “you” separately directs the request for aid to God; the Lord’s Prayer asks the Father for daily bread in the first-person plural.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.13\tasking God for deliverance\tThe commentary joins worship with dependence on God for help; the Lord’s Prayer asks God to deliver the praying community from evil.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.6.24\tone owner, not two\tThe commentary’s ownership section contrasts a person shared by quarrelling owners with one belonging to a single master; Jesus says a slave cannot serve two masters.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rom.6.16\tobedience and enslavement\tThe commentary explains worship as belonging and obedience, while also recalling human enslavement; Paul says people become slaves of the one they obey, whether sin or righteousness.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:1Cor.7.23\tnot owned by humans\tThe commentary contrasts belonging to God with being enslaved by human masters; Paul tells believers bought with a price not to become slaves of people.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Acts.17.24\tcreator of heaven and earth\tThe commentary’s opening praise calls God Lord of the worlds; Paul proclaims the maker of the world as Lord of heaven and earth.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Acts.17.25\tGod does not need human service\tThe commentary says God has no need of a helper; Paul says God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, since he gives life and breath to all.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rom.12.1\twhole life as worship\tThe commentary says service is a state of belonging, not merely a scheduled rite; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and their life as worship.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.4.16\tapproach for timely help\tThe commentary treats aid as an open request addressed to God; Hebrews invites people to approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find help in need.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:1Thess.5.17\tcontinuing prayer\tThe commentary reads both verbs as an ongoing state rather than a past act or future promise; Paul’s instruction to pray continually gives that persistence a Christian practice.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Acts.4.24\tcommunity addresses the creator\tThe commentary’s “we” speaks directly to God; the gathered believers pray together to the Sovereign Lord who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Acts.4.29\tcommunal request for aid\tThe commentary says aid is separately directed to God; the gathered church asks God to enable his servants to speak boldly amid threats.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Gal.6.2\tmutual assistance\tThe commentary notes that aid among humans can be real while God remains the one finally sought; Paul tells believers to bear one another’s burdens.
strong\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Acts.10.26\ta human refuses worship\tThe commentary cites Jesus refusing divine status; when Cornelius falls before Peter, Peter raises him and says he too is only a man.
strong\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Rev.19.10\tan angel redirects worship\tThe commentary describes angels rejecting worship directed to them; John falls before an angel, who refuses it and says to worship God.
strong\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:Heb.1.6\tangels worship the Son\tThe commentary’s cited Qur’anic scene has angels deny being objects of worship; Hebrews instead says all God’s angels are to worship the Son, a direct difference over the recipient.
strong\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:Rev.5.13\tworship of God and the Lamb\tThe commentary insists on address to God alone and cites Jesus’ rejection of being made divine; Revelation depicts every creature giving blessing and honor to the one on the throne and the Lamb.
strong\tincil\tkarsi_anlati\tSBLGNT:John.20.28\tThomas addresses Jesus as God\tThe commentary’s exclusive “you” is addressed to God and notes Jesus rejecting divine status; Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as “my Lord and my God,” making the Christological difference explicit.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:John.10.28\tbelonging and protection\tThe commentary says those who belong to God are protected from the adversary; Jesus describes his sheep as his own and says no one will snatch them from his hand.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:1Pet.2.9\tpeople belonging to God\tThe commentary understands “we” as a community of God’s servants; Peter calls believers God’s own people, set apart to proclaim his acts.
strong\tincil\tyorum_gelenegi\tDidache 8:3\tdaily communal prayer\tThe commentary notes that Fatiha is recited in every prayer, so even an individual says “we”; the Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord’s Prayer three times daily.
strong\ttevrat\tyorum_gelenegi\tTaanit 2a\tprayer as service\tThe commentary distinguishes worship from asking aid while placing both inside prayer; the rabbis interpret “serve him with all your heart” as prayer, treating petition itself as service.
strong\ttevrat\tyorum_gelenegi\tBerakhot 26b\tprayer and sacrifice\tThe commentary says worship exceeds scheduled rites but is spoken within ritual prayer; the Talmud relates the fixed prayers to the daily offerings, preserving a sacrificial dimension of prayer.
strong\ttevrat\tyorum_gelenegi\tPesachim 10:5\teach generation says “we”\tThe commentary’s communal “we” includes earlier generations; the Mishnah teaches each generation to see itself as having come out of Egypt, making inherited history a present first-person identity.
medium\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.56.7\tforeigners pray in God’s house\tThe commentary presents a community whose “we” can include people of distinct backgrounds; Isaiah says the foreigners who join YHWH will be brought to his house of prayer.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.10.19\tprotection from the adversary\tThe commentary connects belonging to God’s servants with protection from Satan; Jesus gives his disciples authority over the enemy’s power and danger.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Matt.7.14\tthe narrow way to life\tThe commentary links service with the straight path and contrasts it with roads that scatter people; Jesus describes the narrow way that leads to life.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Phil.2.10\tkneeling in allegiance\tThe commentary explains service as reaching bodily humility; Paul pictures every knee bending at Jesus’ name, adding a Christian account of universal homage.
medium\tincil\tyorum_gelenegi\tMishnah Berakhot 5:1\tattention before prayer\tThe commentary emphasizes the worshipper’s direct turn toward God; the Mishnah says prayer should begin in solemn focus, with the pious waiting before they pray to direct their hearts.
medium\tincil\tyorum_gelenegi\tAugustine, Confessions 1.1.1\taddress and dependence\tThe commentary says the prayer’s first direct word places God before the speaker’s own action; Augustine opens by addressing God in praise and describes the human heart as restless until it rests in God.
EOF`;
const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd,workdir:"/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation",max_output_tokens:1000});
text(r.output || `exit ${r.exit_code}`);

const cmd = `cat > enrichment/bible/work/s001/discovery/pilot1-20261005/1_5/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.23.2\tshepherd and flock\tThe commentary develops the owner, leading animal, pasture, and vulnerable wanderer within its herd imagery; the psalm names YHWH as shepherd and the speaker as a sheep who lacks nothing.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.23.4\tguided paths\tThe commentary joins the service-path image to a later request for guidance; the shepherd psalm leads the sheep on right paths for his name’s sake.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.23.5\tcomfort and aid in danger\tThe commentary pictures a worn traveler needing support and asks God for help; the psalmist walks through a deadly valley with the shepherd’s rod and staff as comfort.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ezek.34.12\tscattered flock gathered\tThe commentary contrasts a community that knows its owner with strays who lose the way; Ezekiel pictures YHWH searching for scattered sheep and rescuing them from where they have wandered.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ezek.34.16\tlost and weak restored\tThe commentary’s root imagery includes the lost traveler and the herd animal gone astray; YHWH promises to seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind the injured, and strengthen the weak.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.145.19\tGod hears callers\tThe commentary’s augment links direct address to God’s answer to those who call; the psalm says YHWH hears those who call on him and saves them.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:2Chr.20.12\tour eyes on you for help\tThe commentary makes the aid request a separate act addressed to God; Jehoshaphat prays for the whole people, “we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you.”
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:2Chr.20.17\tGod’s aid in the crisis\tThe commentary leaves the need for help open while making God its sole source; after the communal plea, Judah is told to stand and see the salvation YHWH will give.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Ps.24.2\tcreation belongs to God\tThe commentary describes the human speaker as belonging to the Lord of all creation; the psalm says the earth and all who dwell in it belong to YHWH.
strong\ttevrat\tmotif\tWLC:Isa.45.23\tuniversal homage to YHWH\tThe commentary says worship is addressed to God alone; Isaiah’s oracle has every knee bow to YHWH and every tongue swear allegiance to him.
strong\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Exod.4.14\tAaron appointed as helper\tThe commentary recalls Moses asking God for Aaron’s help in the mission to Pharaoh; in Exodus God appoints Aaron to meet Moses and assist him as spokesman.
strong\ttevrat\tparalel\tWLC:Exod.4.15\tGod helps through a human agent\tThe commentary distinguishes asking God for help from receiving human assistance; God tells Moses to speak with Aaron and promises to help both of them speak.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rom.14.8\tlife and death belong to the Lord\tThe commentary says a person belongs to God beyond scheduled acts of worship; Paul says that whether believers live or die, they belong to the Lord.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Phil.4.6\trequest joined to thanksgiving\tThe commentary puts worship and asking aid side by side; Paul tells the community to bring every request to God with thanksgiving, joining petition to praise.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.13.15\tcontinuing sacrifice of praise\tThe commentary says worship is a continuing state and can be spoken in prayer; Hebrews calls believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise through their lips.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:James.1.5\tasking for guidance\tThe commentary moves from “we ask you for aid” to the next verse’s request for guidance; James tells anyone lacking wisdom to ask God, who gives generously.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:1Pet.5.7\tentrusting need to God\tThe commentary leaves the aid requested open to every need; Peter tells believers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.7.9\tone worshipping multitude\tThe commentary reads “we” as a community that reaches beyond a solitary worshipper; Revelation gathers a multitude from every nation before the throne and the Lamb.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.7.15\tGod’s servants before the throne\tThe commentary notes that the soul is first welcomed among God’s servants before entering the garden; Revelation depicts the gathered multitude serving God before his throne day and night.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.7.17\tthe Lamb guides and tends\tThe commentary develops the lost traveler, the herd, and the need for guidance and help; Revelation depicts the Lamb as shepherd leading the people to springs of living water.
strong\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.22.3\tservants in the final dwelling\tThe commentary places the community among God’s servants before naming the garden; Revelation’s final city is where God’s servants worship him and see his face.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.1.14\tangels as sent helpers\tThe commentary says people or other means may assist while God remains the one ultimately asked for help; Hebrews describes angels as spirits sent to serve those who inherit salvation.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rom.8.26\thelp in weakness and prayer\tThe commentary joins aid to worship and prayer; Paul says the Spirit helps believers in weakness and intercedes when they do not know how to pray.
medium\tincil\tparalel\tSBLGNT:Luke.15.4\tthe lost sheep sought\tThe commentary evokes the strayed herd animal and the traveler who cannot find the way; Jesus’ parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Luke.15.5\tthe found sheep carried home\tThe commentary’s image of a vulnerable traveler needing support is made concrete when the shepherd finds the lost sheep, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it home.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Rev.7.16\thunger and thirst relieved\tThe commentary describes asking God for aid across all needs; Revelation says the gathered servants will hunger and thirst no more under the Lamb’s care.
medium\tincil\tmotif\tSBLGNT:Heb.1.14\tservice by intermediaries\tThe commentary distinguishes God as the one asked for help from those who can serve as instruments; Hebrews presents angels as agents sent to aid the heirs of salvation.
EOF`;
const r = await tools.exec_command({cmd,workdir:"/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation",max_output_tokens:1000});
text(r.output || `exit ${r.exit_code}`);
